extracted.intended_audience: researchers and policy‑makers studying grant peer review, scientometrics scholars, and funding agency staff
extracted.subtask_description: Linguistic/statistical analysis of review reports from the 2014 ERC Starting Grants to identify which evaluation dimensions, words/categories, and process factors predict panel scores and selection outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence (ERC stated sole criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Excellence’ should be the only criterion (ERC), but it is unspecific and not operationalized in the ERC guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ERC characterizes excellence with suggested elements (see related entries) but does not operationalize them, intentionally giving panel members freedom; panels therefore interpret and operationalize 'excellence' differently, producing inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project: potential to be groundbreaking / high risk–high gain / interdisciplinarity
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC guidance: 'Projects should be potentially groundbreaking, high risk–high gain, and preferably interdisciplinary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although ERC endorses high‑risk/high‑gain, the paper documents that panels often treat risk negatively (e.g., describing ‘the project may probably fail’) and may penalize risky proposals; interdisciplinarity and groundbreaking claims are suggested but not operationally defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should have developed independence; ERC proposes one yardstick: publications not coauthored with the Ph.D. supervisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews show panel members use alternative indicators (acquired funding, leading a team, topical distance from supervisor, different institutions, new collaborations). The lack of consensus about which indicator to use leads to inconsistent assessment of independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate scoring of Project and PI (in principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels are instructed to give separate scores for the project (proposal) and the PI (CV/track record).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice the paper finds very high correlation between PI and Project scores (r≈0.87 in phase 1), suggesting panelists often do not distinguish between the two dimensions and may adapt one score based on the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track record / past performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of past performance (track record, achievements, publications, grants, collaboration quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational performance indicators used in analyses include normalized journal citation score (NJCS), share of top 5% most cited papers, number of grants, quality of collaboration network (median pp10% of organizations), number of international coauthors, total coauthors, H‑index, etc. The linguistic analysis shows words referring to track record often appear and correlate (moderately) with objective performance measures; more discussion of track record often correlates with lower scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal quality (content of proposed study)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the quality and content of the research proposal (originality, feasibility, methods, timeline, laboratory/multidisciplinary aspects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LIWC 'proposal' category (e.g., laboratory, multidisciplinary, timeline) was tracked. The paper finds more words about the proposal sometimes linked to more disagreement and lower scores (panels often focus on weak points in proposals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk assessment (how risk is treated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement about project risk (whether high risk is treated positively as high‑gain or negatively as likely to fail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although ERC recommends high risk–high gain, panels commonly view risk as negative; examples show panels hesitating that a successful project might 'not be taken up' and thereby lower scores. How panels interpret risk is a substantive dimension affecting funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative evaluation language (negation, negative evaluation, exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of negative linguistic categories: negation words (hasn’t, don’t, can’t), negative evaluation words (naïve, defect*, lack*), and exclusion words (but, either, except, just, not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These negative categories have the strongest (negative) effects on panel scores across phases; their prevalence signals attention to weaknesses and is interpreted as a predictor of rejection. The paper emphasizes panels 'focus on rejecting the applications by searching for weak points.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive evaluation language, superlatives, positive emotions, certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of positive evaluative words (intriguing, compelling), superlatives (world class, outstanding, exceptional, groundbreaking, great potential, high risk high gain), positive emotion words and certainty words (fundamental, commitment, truly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of superlatives and positive evaluation words is positively correlated with higher panel scores (but with smaller standardized effects than negative language). Certainty words appear more in successful applications. Authors added ERC‑specific superlatives to LIWC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agentic / ability / achievement / personal characteristic language
rubrics_metrics.description: Words referring to personal characteristics: agentic words (outspoken, solid, risk), ability words (gift*, intell*, skill*) and achievement words (creati*, excel*, compet*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories index perceptions of the applicant's personal characteristics and ability. In regressions some of these categories had small or non‑significant effects; achievement/agentic/ability were removed in some final models, indicating mixed predictive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel disagreement / consensus (coefficient of variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of disagreement among panelists measured by coefficient of variation (CoV) of scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher panel disagreement negatively affects final scores, particularly strong in the decisive second phase. CoV is used as a control variable in regressions and considered an important process indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational indicators used by reviewers (journal impact factors vs paper quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proxy criteria reviewers use when direct assessment is difficult (e.g., relying on journal impact factors, counts of highly cited papers, or individual high‑quality papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews reveal disagreement among panelists: some evaluate individual papers and citations; others use journal impact factors as a proxy. Reliance on proxies/heuristics varies by panelist and affects consistency and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural constraints and workload (time per proposal, number of reviewers, phases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Process features that influence evaluation: five‑page proposal + five‑page CV in phase 1; typical panel size ≈10; panels handle 80–250 applicants over ≈2 days (<10 min discussion per proposal); typical number of reviews per proposal (phase 1: mostly 4; phase 2: 6–8 external reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severe time pressure and broad panel scope lead reviewers to use heuristics and stereotyping. These process constraints are treated by the authors as determinants of decision quality and a 'criterion' (i.e., the procedure's adequacy) when assessing the fairness and validity of selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: reject‑to‑reduce (focus on identifying weak points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed decision strategy where panels concentrate on rejecting applications by searching for weak points rather than actively selecting high‑risk/high‑gain proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strategy is linked to low predictive validity and potential systematic false negatives; it also explains the dominance of negative linguistic categories in reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bibliometric performance indicators as reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison and correlation of linguistic/report features with bibliometric metrics (NJCS, top‑5% share, grant counts, collaboration quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors use bibliometric indicators as an objective frame of reference. 'Positive' linguistic categories weakly correlate positively with bibliometric performance; 'negative' categories correlate moderately negatively. This supports that panels' negative language often reflects perceived lower past performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic‑category measurement and modeling (LIWC + ERC‑specific dictionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting normalized frequencies of LIWC categories (augmented with case‑specific frequent terms) and using them as predictors in linear regression models (backward removal) to predict panel scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological criterion: preprocessing to remove instruction text, normalization by document length, adding ERC‑specific terms to LIWC, checking multicollinearity (VIF/tolerance), and controlling for disagreement (CoV). The explanatory power (R^2) of models reached ~0.46–0.51 in phase 1.
